question:
Patient note:
A 68-year-old man with stage III chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 1.7 mg/dL three months ago), biopsy-proven hepatitis C cirrhosis with recent onset cholestatic jaundice, non-insulin-dependent diabetes, and a 40-pack-year tobacco history was found collapsed on the living-room floor by a home-health aide who had arrived for a scheduled morning visit; the aide reported the patient had been increasingly somnolent over the preceding 48 hours and complained of dark urine, pruritus, and right upper-quadrant discomfort but had refused to go to clinic. Emergency medical technicians arrived within ten minutes to discover him stuporous, breathing erratically at 34 breaths per minute, saturating 79 % on room air, with gurgling respirations and vomitus in the oropharynx. After a brief attempt at bag-mask ventilation proved ineffective because of poor seal and copious secretions, they performed rapid-sequence orotracheal intubation using ketamine and succinylcholine, inserted a 7.5-mm cuffed tube on the first pass, and connected him to a transport ventilator in assist-control mode delivering a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, a rate of 18, 5 cm H₂O of end-expiratory pressure, and an inspired oxygen fraction set at 0.57. No non-invasive positive-pressure interface had been tried beforehand, and no crystalloid boluses, vasopressors, antibiotics, or vasoactive infusions were started during the eleven-minute ride. On entry to the resuscitation bay—before any hospital therapy had been initiated—vital signs recorded by the automated cuff were 100/59 mm Hg, heart rate 112 beats per minute in sinus tachycardia, respiratory rate equal to the ventilator setting, temperature 38.3 °C via rectal probe, and oxygen saturation fluctuating between 90 % and 92 % on the same 0.57 FiO₂. Extremities were warm with brisk capillary refill, jugular venous distension was absent at 30°, and there was no peripheral mottling. A right radial arterial catheter placed within three minutes produced an arterial blood gas showing pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 41 mm Hg, bicarbonate 19 mEq/L, lactate 3.9 mmol/L, and a PaO₂ of 87 mm Hg on the documented inspired-oxygen fraction. Neurologic evaluation after confirming the paralytic had worn off revealed pupils 3 mm and sluggishly reactive, no spontaneous eye opening, absent verbalization around the inflated cuff, and flexor withdrawal of both upper limbs to a trapezius squeeze, yielding a composite Glasgow Coma Score of 6 without obvious lateralizing deficits. Skin survey disclosed deep scleral icterus, scattered spider angiomas over the upper chest, and multiple petechiae on the lower legs. Breath sounds were diminished bilaterally with coarse crackles in the right base; peak inspiratory pressure measured 26 cm H₂O. Cardiac auscultation was notable only for a grade II/VI systolic flow murmur at the left sternal border. The abdomen was distended but soft, tender maximally in the right upper quadrant, and a positive Murphy sign was elicited despite depressed mentation. A 16-French Foley catheter inserted on arrival immediately drained 35 mL of dark tea-colored urine; collateral information from the home-health log and family notes indicated total urine collection of approximately 420 mL over the preceding 24 hours. Initial laboratory work drawn simultaneously with the arterial sample showed white-blood-cell count 19.2 × 10³/µL with 15 % band forms, hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL, hematocrit 34 %, and a platelet count of 97 000 per microliter. Comprehensive metabolic panel demonstrated sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 5.3 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate mirroring the arterial value, blood urea nitrogen 68 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine markedly elevated at 3.2 mg/dL compared with his last outpatient measurement. Total bilirubin returned at 4.1 mg/dL (direct fraction 3.3 mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase 138 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 121 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 286 U/L, consistent with obstructive and hepatocellular injury. Coagulation profile revealed an international normalized ratio of 1.8 and activated partial-thromboplastin time 44 seconds. High-sensitivity troponin was 0.05 ng/mL with no acute ischemic changes on a 12-lead electrocardiogram. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained while he remained on the initial ventilator settings demonstrated right lower-lobe opacification suggestive of aspiration, elevated hemidiaphragms, and appropriate endotracheal-tube position 3 cm above the carina. Focused abdominal ultrasound performed at the bedside showed a dilated common bile duct measuring 11 mm with intraluminal echogenic material and posterior acoustic shadowing, moderate gallbladder wall thickening, and sluggish flow in the portal vein; the inferior vena cava was collapsible on inspiration, arguing against frank volume overload. Bedside echocardiography depicted hyperdynamic left-ventricular systolic function without segmental wall-motion abnormalities. No intravenous fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, vasopressor agents, renal replacement modalities, sedative infusions, or additional ventilator adjustments had been started at the moment these physiologic and laboratory data were captured; the patient thus remained intubated and mechanically ventilated on 0.57 inspired oxygen with an arterial oxygen tension of 87 mm Hg, perfusing spontaneously at 100/59 mm Hg without pharmacologic support, exhibiting severe thrombocytopenia, significant hyperbilirubinemia, advanced azotemia coupled with oliguria, and deep encephalopathy—all consistent with suspected ascending cholangitis complicated by renal and respiratory failure.

Question: What is the patient's Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) Score?
solution:
SOFA assigns 0–4 points to each of six organ systems. Using the admission measurements:
- Respiratory: PaO₂/FiO₂ = 87/0.57 ≈ 153 mm Hg. A ratio of 100 to <200 on mechanical ventilation scores 3.
- Coagulation: platelets 97,000/µL fall in the 50,000 to <100,000/µL range: 2.
- Liver: total bilirubin 4.1 mg/dL falls in the 2.0–5.9 mg/dL range: 2.
- Cardiovascular: mean arterial pressure = (100 + 2 × 59)/3 ≈ 73 mm Hg. This is ≥70 without vasopressors: 0.
- Neurologic: GCS 6 falls in the 6–9 range: 3.
- Renal: creatinine 3.2 mg/dL scores 2, but urine output of 420 mL/24 h (200 to <500 mL) scores 3. Use the higher renal score: 3.
Total = 3 + 2 + 2 + 0 + 3 + 3 = 13.
Final answer: 13
